content: In 2010, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommended annual influenza vaccination for all individuals aged 6 months and older in the United States. This recommendation remains in place. The ACIP provides updated guidance for the use of influenza vaccines during each flu season, including vaccination schedules for children aged 6 months to 8 years, descriptions of available vaccine products, and specific indications for their use. Additionally, the ACIP addresses febrile seizures associated with influenza and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, vaccination recommendations for individuals with egg allergies, and the development of quadrivalent influenza vaccines for future use. The ACIP Influenza Work Group meets every 2-4 weeks throughout the year to discuss influenza-related issues, including vaccine effectiveness, safety, coverage, program feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and anticipated vaccine supply. Data from the CDC’s Influenza Division, Immunization Safety Office, and Immunization Services Division are reviewed to inform recommendations. Presentations from invited experts and both published and unpublished data are also considered. For the 2012-2013 influenza season, the vaccine contains antigens from A/California/7/2009 (H1N1)-like, A/Victoria/361/2011 (H3N2)-like, and B/Wisconsin/1/2010-like (Yamagata lineage) strains. The H3N2 and B antigens differ from those in the 2010-2011 and 2011-2012 vaccines. The H1N1 component remains the same as that used in the 2009 monovalent pandemic vaccine and subsequent seasonal vaccines. Recommendations for Vaccination Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for all individuals aged 6 months and older. Vaccination should ideally occur before the onset of influenza activity in the community to allow time for the development of protective antibody levels. Providers should offer vaccination as soon as the vaccine becomes available and continue as long as influenza viruses are circulating. Vaccine Dose Considerations for Children Aged 6 Months to 8 Years Children aged 6 months to 8 years require two doses of influenza vaccine during their first season of vaccination, administered at least 4 weeks apart, to optimize immune response. Studies have shown that two doses result in significantly higher protective antibody responses compared to a single dose. For children who have not received a vaccine containing the 2009 H1N1 antigen, two doses are recommended this season, even if they previously received two doses of seasonal influenza vaccine before the 2010-2011 season. Two approaches are acceptable for determining the number of doses required for children in this age group: 1. Consider only doses of seasonal influenza vaccine received since July 1, 2010. Children who received two or more doses since this date need only one dose in 2012-2013. Those who did not require two doses. 2. In settings where vaccination history before the 2010-2011 season is available, children who received two or more doses of seasonal vaccine before July 1, 2010, and at least one dose of monovalent 2009 H1N1 vaccine or seasonal vaccine since July 1, 2010, need only one dose in 2012-2013. Otherwise, two doses are required. Available Vaccine Products and Indications Multiple influenza vaccines with the same antigenic composition are available for the 2012-2013 season. Trivalent inactivated vaccines (TIV) are administered intramuscularly, with the deltoid muscle preferred for adults and older children and the anterolateral thigh for infants and younger children. Fluzone Intradermal is administered intradermally over the deltoid muscle. Age indications for TIV products vary, and providers should consult package inserts for updated information. The live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV), FluMist, is indicated for healthy, non-pregnant individuals aged 2 through 49 years. No preference is expressed for TIV versus LAIV in this age group. Vaccination of Persons with Egg Allergy Persons with a history of mild egg allergy (e.g., hives) should receive TIV with additional precautions, including administration by a healthcare provider familiar with egg allergy manifestations and observation for at least 30 minutes post-vaccination. Those with severe allergic reactions to egg exposure should be referred to an allergist for further risk assessment. All vaccines should be administered in settings equipped to manage anaphylaxis. Febrile Seizures Associated with TIV and PCV13 Febrile seizures are common in young children, with 2%-5% experiencing at least one seizure. During the 2010-2011 influenza season, an increased risk of febrile seizures was observed in children aged 6 months to 4 years on the day of vaccination or the day after, particularly when TIV and PCV13 were co-administered. The risk was lower than that observed in Australia in 2010. No policy changes were recommended for the use of TIV or PCV13 for subsequent seasons. Quadrivalent Influenza Vaccines Currently available influenza vaccines are trivalent, containing antigens from A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and one B lineage. Quadrivalent vaccines, which include antigens from both B lineages (Victoria and Yamagata), are under development to address limited cross-protection between B lineages. A quadrivalent LAIV, FluMist Quadrivalent, was approved in February 2012 and is expected to replace the trivalent formulation for the 2013-2014 season. Inactivated quadrivalent vaccines are also in development and will be addressed in future ACIP statements as they become available.
